title: Cicoria Ripassata
subtitle: Roman wild chicory wilted with garlic, olive oil, and chilli
excerpt: Cicoria ripassata is a Roman way with bitter greens: chicory or dandelion leaves boiled until tender, then tossed briefly in a pan with olive oil, garlic, and chilli. Ripassata means 'passed through the pan again': the second cooking in olive oil and garlic transforms the boiled greens into something much more flavourful. It is a Roman side dish and a meal in itself with bread.
sourceNotes: Cicoria ripassata is a classic Roman dish, documented in the cucina romana tradition as one of the city's most characteristic side dishes. Wild chicory (cicoria selvatica) is gathered from the fields around Rome and is a bitter green deeply embedded in Roman food culture. The ripassata technique: boiling then sautéing: is used across Italian cooking for all types of bitter greens.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Boil the greens up to a day ahead and refrigerate. Do the ripassata stage just before serving.

content.text: Cicoria ripassata is a two-stage method: the greens are boiled first until tender, then briefly fried in olive oil with garlic and chilli. The ripassata stage does all the flavour work: the garlic infuses the oil, the chilli adds heat, and the boiled greens soak up the seasoned fat as they toss in the pan. Use chicory, dandelion leaves, turnip tops, or any bitter leafy green. The bitterness is not a problem to overcome; it is what the dish is about.

items.prepNote: or dandelion greens / turnip tops, tough stems removed

content.text: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Add the chicory and cook for 8 to 12 minutes until completely tender and no longer fibrous. The greens should be soft, not just wilted. Drain and squeeze out as much water as possible with your hands.
Warm the olive oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Add the garlic and chilli. Cook for 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold: do not brown it.

Add the drained chicory to the pan. Toss in the oil and garlic for 3 to 4 minutes over medium-high heat until the greens have absorbed the flavoured oil and smell fragrant. Season with salt. Serve hot or at room temperature with bread.

items.symptom: Greens are still tough after boiling
items.cause: Chicory stalks are fibrous and need longer cooking than the leaves
items.fix: Remove the toughest parts of the stalk before cooking. Mature wild chicory can need 12 to 15 minutes at a rolling boil to become fully tender.

items.cause: Wild chicory has a pronounced bitterness that is an acquired taste
items.fix: Change the boiling water halfway through cooking to leach out more bitterness. The ripassata stage with garlic and oil softens the perception of bitterness significantly.

items.symptom: Greens are watery and don't absorb the olive oil
items.cause: Not enough water was squeezed out after boiling
items.fix: Squeeze the boiled greens very hard: this step is essential. Wet greens steam in the pan rather than fry and never absorb the oil.

content.text: Cicoria ripassata is a Roman institution. Wild chicory is gathered in the fields of the Roman countryside (the Campagna Romana) from autumn through spring and sold in bundles in the city's markets. Roman food culture prizes bitter greens in a way that is unusual by northern European or British standards: the bitterness is valued, not apologised for. The dish appears in Roman trattorie as a contorno (side dish) alongside coda alla vaccinara, abbacchio, and other traditional Roman mains. Eaten with good bread and olive oil it is also a satisfying light lunch in itself.
